# CI (`.github/workflows/`)

- **`test-tools.yml`**: on every PR and push to `main`, runs `npm test` (+ `tsc --noEmit`) for `tools/build-kv`, `tools/publish-kv`, and `edge/`. No secrets needed.
- **`test-starter-kits.yml`**: on every PR, detects which `starter-kits/<lang>/<kit>/` directories changed (`dorny/paths-filter`, grouped into unique `(language, kit)` pairs — an empty result cleanly skips the build job rather than erroring, which a raw empty GitHub Actions matrix would do) and, for each one, builds it the same way a real customer would: via the real Fastly CLI (`fastly/compute-actions/build`), against whatever `fastly.toml` itself declares. Also smoke-tests it (`fastly compute serve`, polling the port rather than grepping stdout, tolerating any HTTP response rather than asserting specific content since several kits have real external backend dependencies a CI runner can't satisfy) and runs the kit's own test suite if it defines one (no kit does, so that step is inert; it can also only meaningfully exercise kit code that doesn't directly depend on the Compute-runtime-only SDKs, since those need Viceroy/a WASI runtime that nothing here configures native `go test`/`cargo test` to use).
  - **`post_init` is NOT run by `fastly compute build`** (only by `compute init`, confirmed via `fastly compute build --help`) — so the workflow runs it explicitly first, via Python's stdlib `tomllib` (never hand-parse TOML — see the `[catalog]` section of the root `CLAUDE.md` for why), unconditionally for every language (the script itself no-ops if a kit declares no `post_init` — true for all **rust** kits today). **cpp** and **javascript** kits need this to set up build tooling the build step then depends on (`cmake --preset wasi`, `npm install`). **go**'s `post_init` (`go get ...@latest`) runs too, deliberately — it does bump the SDK version on every CI run (non-deterministic in that sense), but the shipped tarball omits lockfiles precisely so a customer's first build re-resolves current dependency versions (see the lockfile-omission note in the root `CLAUDE.md`'s pipeline section), so CI needs to exercise that same real path for Go rather than only ever validating the repo's own pinned `go.sum` copy.
  - Toolchains are set up per-kit, not repo-wide: Go via `actions/setup-go` with `go-version-file` (versions vary 1.17–1.23 across kits) except the `tinygo` kit, which needs a newer host Go than its own `go.mod` states (pinned `1.24` — tinygo `0.41.1`'s bundled `net/http` calls `strings.SplitSeq`/`FieldsFuncSeq`, added in Go 1.24's stdlib, despite tinygo's own compat matrix claiming 1.23 support; see [tinygo-org/tinygo#5446](https://github.com/tinygo-org/tinygo/issues/5446)) plus the TinyGo compiler itself (`acifani/setup-tinygo`, pinned `0.41.1`); Rust needs no setup action (`rustup` ships on the runner and auto-installs whatever each kit's own `rust-toolchain.toml` declares); JavaScript uses one pinned Node LTS version for all kits (they don't consistently declare `engines`); C++ needs a pinned WASI SDK release installed to `/opt/wasi-sdk` (currently `wasi-sdk-27`, matching `CMakePresets.json`'s hardcoded toolchain-file path `/opt/wasi-sdk/share/cmake/wasi-sdk-p1.cmake` — **local C++ contributors need a WASI SDK at that same path to match CI**; there's no bundled/official installer for this, it's a manual download+extract).
  - **Python** needs no `setup-python`: `astral-sh/setup-uv` installs `uv`, which provisions a managed CPython matching the kit's own `requires-python` on demand (the kit's `[scripts] build` is `uv run fastly-compute-py build`, so the venv is created by the build itself). The cache key is the kit's `uv.lock`. Python is also the only language whose CI runs a formatter/linter that isn't part of its build — `uvx ruff format --check` + `uvx ruff check`, carried over from the kit's own upstream workflow (`ruff` is not declared as a kit dependency; `uvx` fetches it, so it drifts with upstream releases rather than being pinned).
  - The 6 `fanout`/`fanout-forward` kits (go/js/rust) are exempted from the smoke-test step specifically — they need Pushpin, which `fastly compute serve` only supports experimentally and doesn't bundle. The `auth` kits (js + rust) are exempted as well — they need a secret store configured, which CI does not set up.
  - Stays on plain `pull_request` (never `pull_request_target`), since it builds untrusted fork-PR code with no secrets involved.
- **`main.yml`**: `publish-kv` always runs first on every push to `main`, and `deploy-edge` runs afterward (`needs: publish-kv`) only if `edge/**` changed in that push, or the workflow was manually dispatched with `force_deploy_edge`. Deliberately one workflow with sequential jobs, not two independently `push`-triggered ones — a merge touching both `starter-kits/**` and `edge/**` at once could otherwise let them race, deploying `edge/` against stale/incomplete KV data. For the manual/local equivalent, invoke the `deploy-edge` skill.

# Dependabot (`.github/dependabot.yml`)

**Routine version updates are capped at minor/patch; urgent fixes come through the security-update channel instead.** Every `updates` entry carries `ignore: [{dependency-name: "*", update-types: [version-update:semver-major]}]`. This is deliberate: an ungrouped major bump across 17 JavaScript kits at once (react 18→19 + typescript 5→7 + eslint 8→10 + babel 7→8 in one PR) is not reviewable, and these are customer-facing sources that must stay buildable. The escape hatch is that `update-types` ignore conditions apply to **version updates only, never to security updates** — so anything with a real advisory still raises a PR regardless of the cap. That only works because *Dependabot security updates are enabled on the repo* (`GET /repos/fastly/compute-starter-kits/automated-security-fixes`); if that setting ever gets switched off, the cap silently becomes "no urgent fixes at all."

- **The 0.x minor caps are a separate rule, not redundancy.** Under Cargo's compatibility rules (and npm's de-facto equivalent) a `0.22 → 0.23` bump is breaking, but Dependabot still classifies it as `semver-minor`, so the major cap above does not catch it. Hence the extra per-name `semver-minor` ignores: `base64`/`hex`/`jwt-simple`/`rand`/`time` for cargo, `cookie`/`esbuild`/`process` for the JavaScript kits. **These lists are hand-maintained** — a new 0.x direct dependency in any kit needs adding, or its breaking minors flow through unchecked.
- **Python uses the `uv` ecosystem, not `pip`.** `uv` is its own `package-ecosystem` value and is what reads `pyproject.toml` + `uv.lock`; `pip` covers requirements.txt/pipenv/poetry instead. No 0.x minor cap list is needed for it yet — `fastly-compute` is 0.x but deliberately uncapped like the other Fastly SDKs, and `flask` is 3.x, so the wildcard major cap already covers it. A new 0.x direct dependency in a Python kit would need adding, same as the cargo/npm lists.
- **The Fastly SDK exemption is only partial, and cannot be made complete.** `ignore.dependency-name` has no negation syntax and two `updates` entries may not share an ecosystem + directory, so "wildcard except Fastly" is inexpressible. Where it *is* expressible it's applied: `fastly`, `log-fastly`, `@fastly/compute-js-context` and `@fastly/hono-fastly-compute` are all 0.x and deliberately omitted from the 0.x minor lists, so their minors keep flowing. What the wildcard does still block is a hypothetical `@fastly/js-compute` 4.0 or `compute-sdk-go` v2 — both coordinated all-kits-at-once bumps to drive by hand anyway (and a Go `v2` needs a `/v2` import path rewrite Dependabot handles poorly regardless).
- **`directories` globs must point at a manifest, not its parent.** The npm entry says `tools/*`, not `tools` — there is no `tools/package.json`, so `tools` matched nothing and `tools/build-kv`/`tools/publish-kv` went years without a single update PR while still showing up in the dependency graph's alerts. A glob that matches nothing fails silently; there is no warning anywhere.
- Each entry also declares a `*` group with `applies-to: security-updates`, so the security channel arrives as a few consolidated PRs (Dependabot merges across an entry's `directories`) rather than one PR per advisory per kit. Note `open-pull-requests-limit` defaults to 5 per entry, so a large backlog lands in waves.
- The cap applies to `github-actions` too, for consistency with the other ecosystems. The tradeoff there is different, though — GHA majors are how runner/Node upgrades arrive, so staying capped eventually means running deprecated action versions. Deleting that one entry's `ignore` block is the fix if the churn turns out to be worth it.
